bibliographic.title: Navigating AI governance for oncology nursing: Existing models, implications, and a Call for nurse-led oversight in Asia Pacific health systems
bibliographic.citation_apa: Adapa, K., & Jayakumar, N. (2026). Navigating AI governance for oncology nursing: Existing models, implications, and a Call for nurse-led oversight in Asia Pacific health systems. Asia-Pacific Journal of Oncology Nursing, 13, 100964. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apjon.2026.100964

methodology.method_family: commentary with critical policy and framework overview
methodology.technology_context: Broad AI in oncology including machine learning imaging, natural language processing on clinical notes, predictive analytics, and clinical documentation automation; governance models include EU AI Act, WHO Ethics Guidance, NAM AI Code of Conduct, and IMDRF Good Machine Learning Practice

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article is a peer-reviewed commentary on AI governance for oncology nursing in Asia Pacific health systems. It strongly addresses regulated healthcare governance, human oversight, accountability, risk-based regulation, and lifecycle monitoring, but does not study or propose governance for conversational LLM systems, chatbots, agents, RAG, guardrails, observability, or post-deployment operational controls specific to generative conversational AI. Generative AI appears only in the authors' writing-process declaration.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Automated triage graded this as a central candidate, but full text indicates a non-empirical healthcare governance commentary without conversational LLM focus; adjudication should confirm contextual versus central placement.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate as normative commentary mapping regulatory and ethical frameworks to nursing practice, but offers no empirical sampling, primary data collection, or evaluation of conversational AI systems. Limitations of the commentary approach are not explicitly discussed in the provided excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: The argument is coherent and adequately supported for a policy commentary on nurse-led AI governance in regulated oncology care, but methodological limitations are substantial for empirical synthesis and relevance to conversational LLM governance is only partial.

coding.theme: AI governance integration with oncology nursing in regulated health systems
coding.subtheme: nurse-led human oversight across the cancer care pathway

synthesis.main_claim: As AI becomes operational in Asia Pacific oncology care, governance must move beyond technology-centric oversight to deliberate nurse-led mechanisms that position nurses as the essential human control layer for safe, equitable, patient-centred AI use.
synthesis.contribution: Critically overviews major AI governance models relevant to nursing and translates them into eight actionable recommendations for health system leaders, policymakers, and nurse executives in oncology settings.
synthesis.limitations: Commentary without new data or empirical evaluation; focuses on broad clinical AI rather than conversational or LLM-specific systems; limitations of the commentary itself are not clearly stated in the provided text.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence on human oversight, accountability, and multi-layer governance in regulated healthcare. Do not treat as central evidence on conversational governance of LLM-based systems.

evidence.claim: The text reviews existing governance models including the EU AI Act, WHO Ethics Guidance, and NAM AI Code of Conduct.
evidence.excerpt: This commentary examines existing AI governance models—from the EU AI Act to the World Health Organization (WHO) Ethics Guidance and the NAM AI Code of Conduct

evidence.claim: Governance gap includes pre-deployment evaluation, in-workflow guidance, and post-implementation monitoring.
evidence.excerpt: lack of clear mechanisms to evaluate AI systems before deployment, guide their use within clinical workflows, and monitor their performance once implemented

evidence.claim: Oncology AI examples include machine learning imaging and NLP on clinical notes, not conversational LLM systems.
evidence.excerpt: AI applications range from machine learning models that detect early-stage tumours on imaging to natural language processing tools that extract prognostic data from unstructured clinical notes

evidence.claim: EU AI Act is described as a risk-based regulatory framework with human oversight requirements relevant to clinical AI.
evidence.excerpt: It employs a risk-based classification system: AI systems used in medical devices, clinical decision support, and emergency triage

evidence.claim: IMDRF GMLP emphasizes development, validation, and lifecycle monitoring of AI-enabled medical devices.
evidence.excerpt: Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) guidance establishes 10 harmonised principles for the development, validation, and lifecycle monitoring of AI-enabled medical devices.

evidence.claim: Accountability depends on nurse documentation of interaction with AI and clinical reasoning.
evidence.excerpt: the nurse's documentation of their interaction with the AI system, their clinical reasoning in accepting or modifying the recommendation, and their communication with the patient become critical elements of accountability

evidence.claim: Eight actionable recommendations are offered to leaders and policymakers.
evidence.excerpt: Eight actionable recommendations are offered for health system leaders, policymakers, and nurse executives.
